text:
From 2% to 10%.
That is the share of the map around one community where it now ranks in Google's top three.

This is an apartment community we work with in Nevada, on a common renter search in its city. In early October it made the top three map results in about 2% of the surrounding area. A week later it was about 10%, and it held there in each of the next three weekly checks.

Where it does show up, its average spot moved from around 10th to around 3rd.

I want to be honest about the other 90%. Across most of the area it still sits outside the top three, and a busy city search is a crowded one. I also can't point to a single cause. Map results move with reviews, profile activity, distance and what competitors do.

What I like is that it held. One good week is noise. Four in a row starts to look like footing.

How do you track where your community shows up beyond the leasing office?

text:
The first week with a new marketing partner decides more than the contract does.
Most of it comes down to what you hand over on day one.

Budget season is when a lot of communities switch agencies or add one. The handoff tends to get treated like paperwork. In my experience it is the part that decides how fast the work gets good.

Five things worth handing over on day one:
1. The real photos, and a note on which ones are renderings.
2. The current special, word for word, and who approves changes to it.
3. The fee sheet and pet policy your leasing team actually quotes.
4. The questions renters ask most, straight from the leasing office.
5. Access to the Google profile, with your company as the owner.

None of it is glamorous. All of it shows up in the first month of posts, listings and answers renters see.

When we start with a community, we check Google Search, Google Maps and AI answers and send a clear plan to close the gaps.

documentTitle: Before the doors open: what renters look for in a lease up
text:
A lease up gets marketed long before the first tour.
Renters start forming an opinion the day a new building shows up online.

That first impression often comes from places a team hasn't gotten to yet: a Google profile with a few construction photos, a floor plan page that says coming soon, a social feed that stopped posting after the groundbreaking.

The swipe walks through five things renters tend to look for before a community opens, and what each one can say while the details are still being finalized.

The thread running through all five is honesty: renderings labeled as renderings, a price or a plain line about when it will be posted, and a tour option that is easy to find.

Our lease up guide breaks the work into before, during and after opening. LocalLift, our weekly Google, Maps and AI visibility program, is built to keep working after the launch budget ends.

The shortlist is built online now.
For most renters, the decision still gets made standing in the apartment.

Renters may narrow a search on Google Maps, listing sites, reviews and, more and more, AI assistants. By the time someone books a tour, the comparison is often down to two or three places.

That changes what the tour has to do. It is less of an introduction and more of a check: does this place match what I saw online?

When the photos, the price and the details line up with what the renter found, the tour can confirm a decision that is already half made. When they don't, even a great tour starts by explaining the difference.

That is why we see online visibility and the in person experience as one job. Through LocalLift, we look at renter trust as closely as we look at getting found.

Some renters sign a lease in a city they have never visited.
They decide almost entirely from what they can see online.

Think of a nurse starting a job across the country, or someone relocating for work. Plenty of people choose an apartment from hundreds of miles away, with one quick visit or none at all.

They need context a local already has: what the drive to work looks like at 8 AM, where guests can park on a weeknight, how far the grocery store really is. A polished amenity photo rarely answers that. A plain video walking from parking to the front door answers a lot.

text:
A lot of apartment reels lose viewers in the first second.
Many of them open on the lobby.

A wide, slow pan across a beautiful lobby is how a lot of community videos start. It looks great in the edit. On a phone, it can read like an ad, and people tend to keep scrolling before the good part arrives.

The openings that seem to hold attention are smaller and more human. A door opening into afternoon light. Keys landing on a counter. A dog pulling toward the park. Someone stepping onto a balcony with a coffee. Something happens in the first second, and the viewer wants to see what comes next.

The lobby can still appear. It just works better as the payoff than the opening.

At The SocialDM we produce reels and photo posts for each community every week, so we think about that first second a lot.

text:
28 new Google reviews in about five weeks.
13 of them mention the maintenance team.

This is an apartment community we work with, and the reviews came in between early October and November 10. Twenty seven are five stars, one is a one star, and the overall rating has held at 4.8.

The part I keep coming back to is who the reviews thank. Nearly half mention maintenance, often a friendly, helpful person who fixed something. Renters reading them learn something a tour can't easily show: what happens after move in.

That is a useful reminder for any team running a review ask. The leasing desk is one moment to ask. Right after a work order is closed may be an even better one, because that is when a resident has just seen how the place takes care of them.

What part of living at your community do your reviews mention most?
